title: Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi Blunts Russia's Drive to Enclose the Donbas
excerpt: A four-phase counteroffensive launched in May has pushed Russian forces back north of Lyman, handed Moscow its worst month of net territorial gains since 2023, and proved maneuver warfare can still work under drone-saturated skies.
body:
• Ukraine's months-long counteroffensive in northern Donetsk — Operation Vivaldi, kept secret until September — has pushed Russian forces back and disrupted Moscow's plan to encircle the Donbas "fortress belt" anchored on Sloviansk and Kramatorsk.
  • The operation, launched May 22 with Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps exploiting gaps in two Russian armies' flanks, reclaimed between 125 and 176 square kilometers; Kyiv says it took 250 Russian prisoners and inflicted over 5,000 casualties.
  • September was Russia's worst month for net territorial gains since June 2023: geolocated data shows Russian forces captured about 175 sq km while losing roughly 256 sq km — a net loss of 81 sq km — despite Putin's claim of 1,301 sq km seized.
  • Fighting remains intense in southern Donbas, and ISW's October 7-8 assessments show Ukrainian forces still advancing on multiple sectors while Russian attacks produced no confirmed territorial gains.

A Counteroffensive Kept Secret for Months

For months, Ukraine was running an offensive in the Donbas that few knew existed. Operation Vivaldi — a four-phase counteroffensive launched on May 22 in northern Donetsk Oblast — was kept largely secret until September, when Kyiv began confirming what the frontline maps were already showing: Ukrainian troops were retaking territory and, more importantly, dismantling a Russian plan to surround the region's last Ukrainian-held cities.

https://x.com/front_ukrainian/status/2108522424102744107

The Russian plan, described in a New York Times analysis, was a wide encirclement of what Ukrainian forces call the Donbas "fortress belt" — the defensive line centered on Sloviansk and Kramatorsk. Moscow intended to approach the two cities from the north through the Lyman sector while advancing from the south, closing the pincer. Operation Vivaldi broke the northern arm. Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps found and exploited gaps along the flanks of Russia's 20th and 25th combined-arms armies, broke into their rear, and forced a pullback across the Zherebets River to avoid encirclement — severing Russian logistical routes and compelling Moscow to redeploy units to stabilize the front.

The Numbers, With Caveats

President Volodymyr Zelensky initially said Ukrainian forces had reclaimed 176 square kilometers (68 square miles) during the operation, later offering a more conservative 125 to 140 square kilometers. Ukraine's presidential office reported that by September 30 — with three of four phases complete — Vivaldi had returned 176 square kilometers to Ukrainian control, taken 250 Russian prisoners, and inflicted more than 5,000 Russian killed and wounded. Kyiv itself noted the figures have not been independently verified, and battlefield accounting in an active war zone is inherently contested.

What is independently verified is the direction of travel. Geolocated evidence tallied by the Institute for the Study of War shows that in September, Russian forces captured about 175 square kilometers while losing roughly 256 square kilometers to Ukrainian operations — a net loss of about 81 square kilometers, making it Moscow's worst month for net territorial gains since June 2023, according to the Kyiv Post's account of the ISW data. Putin, by contrast, told officials Russia had seized 1,301 square kilometers in September — a figure offered without independently verifiable evidence that independent battlefield maps did not support.

"When a military lays the necessary groundwork, mechanized movement remains possible even under dense drone surveillance."

— George Barros, senior analyst, Institute for the Study of War, on Operation Vivaldi

Why Vivaldi Matters Beyond the Map

The operation's significance is partly doctrinal. The drone-saturated battlefield was widely assumed to make maneuver warfare nearly impossible; Vivaldi suggests that carefully planned armored and mechanized movement can still work, as Barros noted — though it also shows the cost, with months of preparation buying back a small fraction of lost territory.

It also undercuts the Kremlin's narrative. Putin has repeatedly claimed Ukraine's Donbas defenses will collapse and that Russian forces will seize the region faster than Kyiv expects. The current front shows something else: in ISW's October 7-8 assessments, Ukrainian forces advanced east of Oleksandrivka in Donetsk, controlled the borderland settlements of Novoplatonivka, Hrekivka, and Druzheliubivka across Kharkiv and Luhansk (a fact acknowledged by a source associated with Russia's own Western forces grouping), and cleared about 10 square kilometers of forest east of Vovchansk, knocking out three Russian infiltration groups. Russian attacks across most of the front produced no confirmed territorial gains.

What Comes Next

The picture is not one-way. Fighting remains intense in southern Donbas, where Russian forces press toward Dobropillia and Kostiantynivka, and ISW notes Russian troops have infiltrated parts of the Vovchansk pocket even as Ukraine advances elsewhere. Moscow's strategic goals have not changed: full control of the Donbas — by force or through Ukrainian concessions — remains Putin's stated condition for ending the war, and Kyiv has rejected Trump administration proposals to cede territory Russia failed to conquer on the battlefield. Overnight on October 6-7, Russia launched a massive combined drone and missile strike across Ukraine that killed and wounded at least 135 civilians, including four children, per ISW — a reminder that battlefield setbacks tend to be answered with strikes on cities. Vivaldi's fourth phase, and Ukraine's ability to hold what it has retaken, will decide whether this autumn's reversal becomes a turning point or a footnote.
